# Routing model traffic with Jev and agentgateway

Put a classifier in front of model selection so each request goes to the cheapest model that can handle it. Rewrite the model in the request body from an ExtProc server, watch three different failures behave three different ways, then build a cache, measure what it got wrong, and take it out again.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=jev-model-routing&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

Eligible paid Zenable customers get an OpenRouter key automatically in their sandbox. Take the hosted version of this lab, with the key already configured, at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=jev-model-routing&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme.

**Duration** 82 minutes · **Difficulty** Advanced

## Set up AI inference

Your sandbox has no hosted AI key. Automatic keys require an eligible paid plan and an available inference budget. Choose your own OpenRouter key, or use the local model and the lab's recorded-answer steps.

### Option A: use your own OpenRouter key

Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys). Then run this in the sandbox terminal, with your key in place of `sk-or-...`:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference sk-or-...
```

The command writes your key and the model settings into `~/.env` and configures every coding agent installed on the sandbox. Open a new terminal so your shell picks them up.

> [!WARNING]
> Your key goes in `~/.env`, never in the lab directory. Every attendee in the sandbox network can read the lab remote, and a key committed there is a key you've shared.

### Option B: use local Ollama (no key)

The sandbox runs [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) with a small model, `qwen3-nothink`, already downloaded and built. Point every agent at it:

```bash
zenable-configure-inference --ollama
```

Then open a new terminal. The model runs on the sandbox's CPU, so expect slower and weaker answers than a hosted model gives you. This option configures coding agents only. For steps that call Jev directly, follow the lab's recorded-answer instructions, such as adding `--fixtures` where shown. Those commands do not switch to recordings automatically.

<details>
<summary>Not on a Zenable sandbox?</summary>

For Option B, install Ollama from [ollama.com/download](https://ollama.com/download). `qwen3:1.7b` is a reasoning model, and thinking makes it very slow on a CPU, so the steps below build a copy with thinking turned off.

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

Then set the variables below in your environment, for example in a `~/.env` file that your shell loads with `set -a; . ~/.env; set +a`. Claude Code reads the `ANTHROPIC_*` variables, and agents that speak the OpenAI API, such as Codex, read `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

## Getting started

_~8 min · Hands-on_

Let's get the repository and its two models:

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
uv sync --locked --project router
```

Both models run on your own machine through Ollama, and the gateway calls them from inside a container. Let's configure Ollama to listen on all interfaces so it can be accessed from the gateway's container.

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d
printf '[Service]\nEnvironment="OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434"\n' \
  | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/listen.conf > /dev/null
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ollama
timeout 90 bash -c 'until curl -fsS http://localhost:11434/api/version >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done'
```

Now let's pull two different models that we'll route between:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:0.6b
```

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

> [!WARNING]
> Run each pull on its own and let it finish, because the progress display swallows anything pasted behind it.

If you're running the Zenable sandbox environments, you already have `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` properly configured; otherwise you will need to set the env vars to ensure access to Jev. If this terminal has been open since the sandbox started, open a new one: the key lands a few seconds after the desktop appears, and only terminals opened after that see it.

The router's settings live in `router.env`, and it's where we turn knobs later.

<details>
<summary>Running without a Jev key?</summary>

Skip this on a Zenable sandbox: the key is already configured and the router asks Jev live. If you have no key, replay the decisions recorded from a real run instead:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
echo 'JEV_FIXTURES=1' > router.env
```

</details>

Now let's bring up our agentgateway stack with a baseline configuration:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
cp 01-baseline.yaml config.yaml
docker buildx use default
docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

```console
NAME           IMAGE                      COMMAND                  SERVICE        CREATED         STATUS                   PORTS
agentgateway   jev-routing-agentgateway   "/app/agentgateway -…"   agentgateway   5 seconds ago   Up 2 seconds (healthy)   127.0.0.1:4000->4000/tcp
jev-router     jev-routing-jev-router     "uv run --no-sync py…"   jev-router     5 seconds ago   Up 4 seconds (healthy)   9090/tcp
```

You should see two containers running; the gateway running and available on port 4000 from your host, and the jev model router available only from inside the docker network.

> [!NOTE]
> If the router doesn't come up as healthy, open a new terminal and run the compose command again. If that doesn't work, check its log with `docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -5`. On a Zenable sandbox, also run `cat ~/.zenable-inference-pickup.log`; if you aren't seeing `zenable: sandbox inference configured` there, please report this to your instructor.

We're going to send a pair of requests numerous times, so let's stash them in some files:

```bash
cat > mechanical.json <<'EOF'
{"model":"auto","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Rename the variable `cfg` to `config` in src/app.py and update the two call sites."}]}
EOF
cat > deliberative.json <<'EOF'
{"model":"auto","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Our checkout service times out under load about once an hour and the logs show no errors. How should we work out what is going wrong?"}]}
EOF
```

Neither one names a model. Send them both:

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
```

```console
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:0.6b
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:0.6b
```

Both land on the small model, because `auto` resolves to `qwen-small`. That's cheap, and diagnosing an hourly timeout on a 0.6B model is where it goes wrong. Pointing `auto` at `qwen-large` instead would fix the diagnosis and pay large-model prices for the rename.

## Putting a classifier in front of model selection

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Here's how we're using the decision model to pick between our two models:

```json
{
  "question": "Which model should answer `request.newest_message`? Judge only the newest message; `request.prior_turns` is context for what it refers to, never the thing being routed.",
  "focus": "Decide on the reasoning the answer needs, not on the topic, the tone, or the length of `request.newest_message`. A request that names the exact edit to make needs no deliberation even when the edit is large. A request that states a goal and leaves the approach open needs deliberation even when it is one sentence.",
  "models": [
    {
      "name": "qwen-small",
      "criterion": "The newest user message asks for a mechanical transformation that a competent engineer would finish without stopping to think: renaming or reformatting code, converting between two named formats, extracting values that are already written down in the message, translating prose, or answering a single factual question whose answer the message already contains. Length alone does not qualify a request for this option; a long but mechanical request still belongs here."
    },
    {
      "name": "qwen-large",
      "criterion": "The newest user message cannot be answered until something is worked out first: weighing a trade-off between two approaches, designing something that does not exist yet, diagnosing a fault from evidence that does not name the cause, reasoning about consequences the message does not state, or producing code whose correctness depends on a rule that has to be derived. Shortness does not disqualify a request from this option; a one-line question can still need deliberation."
    }
  ]
}
```

Both criteria spend their last sentence on the boundary case, because Jev reads them literally and length is the first thing it reaches for as a stand-in for difficulty when nothing rules that out.

Attach the router to the gateway using `02-routed.yaml`, specifically this addition:

```yaml
llm:
  policies:
    extProc:
      host: jev-router:9090
      failureMode: failOpen
      processingOptions:
        requestHeaderMode: send
        responseHeaderMode: skip
        requestBodyMode: buffered
        responseBodyMode: none
        requestTrailerMode: skip
        responseTrailerMode: skip
```

`requestBodyMode: buffered` is important because the default delivers the body in pieces but the router needs all of it before there's JSON to parse.

```bash
cp 02-routed.yaml config.yaml
docker compose restart agentgateway
docker compose up -d --wait agentgateway
```

> [!WARNING]
> Attaching an ExtProc policy needs a restart. Copy the file over and the admin API will show the new policy within a second, while the data plane continues using the old approach until it's reloaded.

Now the same two requests, plus the second one again:

```bash
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
```

```console
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @mechanical.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:0.6b
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:1.7b
$ curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @deliberative.json | jq -r .model
qwen3:1.7b
```

Success! 🎉 We automatically routed different requests to different models just based off of the prompt.

Let's check out the routing logs:

```bash
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'route ->' | tail -3
```

```console
15:03:12 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-small  src=jev      conf=0.99 {'qwen-small': 0.99, 'qwen-large': 0.01}
15:03:13 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-large  src=jev      conf=1.00 {'qwen-small': 0.0, 'qwen-large': 1.0}
15:03:13 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-large  src=exact    conf=1.00 {'qwen-small': 0.0, 'qwen-large': 1.0}
```

Note the third says `src=exact`; it didn't have to call Jev because it already saw this exact request before so it used the cached answer.

The router also sets an `x-jev-route` header carrying the model, the source and the confidence, so the decision travels with the request into whatever reads your traces.

## Handling failures

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Let's dig into the request path itself now; first we'll point the router to a dead end and see what happens:

```bash
echo 'JEV_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9099' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
```

```console
$ echo 'JEV_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9099' >> router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
http=200  total=0.085234s
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
15:03:15 WARNING jev_router.decide jev call failed, routing to qwen-small: All connection attempts failed
15:03:15 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-small  src=fallback conf=0.00
```

The request still completed, and quickly, because the connection was refused right away. The router logged a WARNING and fell back to `qwen-small`, so our deliberative question went to the small model.

Now let's stop the router entirely, so agentgateway's `failOpen` has to handle it:

```bash
docker compose stop jev-router
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
docker compose start jev-router
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait agentgateway
```

```console
$ docker compose stop jev-router
 Container jev-router Stopping
 Container jev-router Stopped
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
http=200  total=10.107756s
$ docker compose start jev-router
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait agentgateway
[+] Running 2/2
 ✔ Container jev-router    Healthy
 ✔ Container agentgateway  Healthy
```

Still a 200, and slower (ten seconds in our run): agentgateway kept trying to look up the stopped router's address, and only after that lookup failed did `failureMode` let the request through. `failureMode` decides whether the request survives, but has no say in how long that takes.

agentgateway also holds on to that failed lookup after the router is back, so the last command recreates agentgateway to make it look the router up again. Without it, every request from here on would skip the router and you'd see no new lines in its log.

Because the router never ran, the body still said `"model": "auto"` when it reached agentgateway's model router. That's why both configs define an `auto` virtual model: it's where requests land when the router is out of the picture.

The third failure is the sneaky one. Let's start a stand-in for Jev that accepts the connection, reads the request, and then never answers:

```bash
nohup uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.standin --mode hang > standin.log 2>&1 &
sleep 2
echo 'JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS=600' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
```

We also raised the router's deadline to ten minutes so it won't rescue us. Ok, now let's send a request into the void:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' --max-time 15 http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
```

```console
http=000  total=15.001343s
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 15001 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
```

The client gave up after fifteen seconds with no bytes received. `failOpen` never fired because, from agentgateway's point of view, nothing failed: the router is connected, healthy, and still thinking.

agentgateway has this open as [issue #3412](https://github.com/agentgateway/agentgateway/issues/3412), and today agentgateway's per-message timeout is ignored, so no gateway setting would have saved this request. The deadline has to live in the router. Let's put it back:

```bash
sed -i '/JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS/d' router.env
echo 'JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS=1.5' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
```

```console
$ sed -i '/JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS/d' router.env
$ echo 'JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS=1.5' >> router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}  total=%{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @deliberative.json
http=200  total=1.607945s
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | tail -2
15:04:36 WARNING jev_router.decide jev call failed, routing to qwen-small: TimeoutError
15:04:36 INFO    jev_router.server route -> qwen-small  src=fallback conf=0.00
```

Now that the router has its deadline back, the same request to the same hung Jev stand-in completes on the fallback model after 1.5 seconds, with a `TimeoutError` in the log.

Question: the first failure added almost no delay and the second added ten seconds. Both answered 200 with the same `failOpen` setting. What made the difference?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

How the far end was unreachable. A closed port refuses the connection immediately, while a hostname that no longer resolves burns through the resolver's timeout first.

Also worth noting: if Jev is down for ten minutes, every routed request pays the full 1.5 second deadline for ten minutes. A circuit breaker that opens after a few consecutive failures and goes straight to the fallback would turn that back into the near-instant refusal we saw first. Agentgateway doesn't have one as of the writing of this lab, however it is something we'd strongly suggest anytime you're depending on a third party in your code's critical path.

</details>

Let's stop the stand-in and reset the router before the next section:

```bash
pkill -f jev_router.standin || true
sed -i '/JEV_BASE_URL/d;/JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS/d' router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
```

## Decision speedups using caching

_~13 min · Hands-on_

We already saw the cache work when a repeated request came back as `src=exact`. That cache keys on the exact message plus everything else sent to Jev, so it only hits when traffic repeats.

The router also has a second cache level which is off by default, keyed on *features* of the request instead: what the message asks for, how long it is, whether it carries code, how many tools came with it, and how deep the conversation runs. Two requests that look alike share a key. Let's switch it on:

```bash
echo 'ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET=1' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
```

```console
$ echo 'ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET=1' >> router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
15:04:40 INFO    jev_router.server ext_proc listening on 0.0.0.0:9090 | jev=jev-latest | deadline=1.5s | cache exact=True bucket=True ttl=900s | policy=6ecdbc563f806f13
```

Two curls won't tell us much about a cache, so the lab repository ships a synthetic week of coding-assistant traffic: twenty-two kinds of work, each asked three different ways.

First, let's ask Jev about every distinct message once so we have a reference answer to grade the cache against:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure oracle
```

```console
asked Jev about 66 distinct messages
wrote oracle.json under policy 6ecdbc563f806f13
```

> [!NOTE]
> If that command printed a traceback instead, the stand-in from the previous section is probably still running: scroll back up to the end of Handling failures and run the block that stops it and resets the router, then try again.

<details>
<summary>Running without a Jev key?</summary>

Skip this if the command above ran. Without a key there's nothing to ask, so copy the answers the repository ships instead:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
cp router/jev_router/fixtures/oracle.json router/oracle.json
```

</details>

Now let's replay two hundred requests, weighted so some messages repeat often, through both cache levels and count the hits:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure replay --stream zipf
```

```console
corpus: deliberative 90, mechanical 110

stream zipf: 200 requests over 45 distinct messages

cache           keys    hit%  jev calls
exact             45   77.5%         45
exact+bucket      12   94.0%         12
```

The feature bucket took the hit rate from 77.5% to 94%. Before we keep it, let's check whether those hits were the right answers:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure replay --stream zipf --grade
```

```console
corpus: deliberative 90, mechanical 110

stream zipf: 200 requests over 45 distinct messages
graded against one fresh answer per distinct message

cache           keys    hit%  jev calls  agree on hits
exact             45   77.5%         45         100.0%
exact+bucket      12   94.0%         12          54.8%

5 buckets held requests that route two different ways:
  read|xs|prose|none|first     {'qwen-large': 27, 'qwen-small': 53}
  other|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-large': 13, 'qwen-small': 23}
  reason|s|prose|none|first    {'qwen-large': 17, 'qwen-small': 3}
  write|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 7, 'qwen-large': 1}
  edit|s|prose|none|first      {'qwen-large': 1, 'qwen-small': 5}
whichever request lands first owns the bucket until the entry expires
```

On a two-option choice, agreeing on about half of the hits is no better than guessing.

Look at the last block. Each of those buckets holds requests that Jev routes to different models. The first request to arrive sets the bucket's answer, and every later request in that bucket gets the same answer until the entry expires. So the bucket cache hit often because the traffic repeated, not because requests in the same bucket need the same model.

The exact cache has no such problem, it only serves a cached answer when the new request is identical to the one Jev already answered. So let's turn the bucket cache back off:

```bash
sed -i '/ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET/d' router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
```

```console
$ sed -i '/ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET/d' router.env
$ docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
 Container jev-router Recreate
 Container jev-router Recreated
 Container jev-router Starting
 Container jev-router Started
 Container jev-router Waiting
 Container jev-router Healthy
$ docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
15:04:46 INFO    jev_router.server ext_proc listening on 0.0.0.0:9090 | jev=jev-latest | deadline=1.5s | cache exact=True bucket=False ttl=900s | policy=6ecdbc563f806f13
```

`bucket=False`, and the router is back to exact matches only.

<details>
<summary>Look closer: what happens when the traffic stops repeating</summary>

Replay the same corpus with every message sent exactly once:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.measure replay --stream unique --grade
```

```console
corpus: deliberative 36, mechanical 30

stream unique: 66 requests over 66 distinct messages
graded against one fresh answer per distinct message

cache           keys    hit%  jev calls  agree on hits
exact             66    0.0%         66              -
exact+bucket      13   80.3%         13          71.7%

5 buckets held requests that route two different ways:
  other|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 11, 'qwen-large': 4}
  read|xs|prose|none|first     {'qwen-small': 5, 'qwen-large': 5}
  write|xs|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 3, 'qwen-large': 3}
  edit|s|prose|none|first      {'qwen-small': 2, 'qwen-large': 2}
  reason|s|prose|none|first    {'qwen-small': 1, 'qwen-large': 1}
whichever request lands first owns the bucket until the entry expires
```

With no repeats, the exact cache hits nothing. The bucket cache still hits most of the traffic and is still wrong about a large slice of it. Run both replays against a week of your own gateway's access log before trusting either number.

</details>

Question: you ran two replay commands, one that counts hits and one that grades them. Which one can you run on your own traffic today?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The hit-rate replay. It only counts cache keys, so it runs on any log of request bodies. It doesn't need a judgement, but on its own it points you at the bucket key.

Conversely, the grading replay needs an oracle first, which is one fresh Jev answer for each distinct message. This shows you whether your cache key carries any routing signal or is just hitting because the traffic repeats.

</details>

## Tuning the routing criteria

_~12 min · Hands-on_

So far we've graded the cache against Jev. Now let's grade Jev itself. Every message family in the corpus carries a hand-written label saying which model it should go to, so let's compare:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align grade --corpus corpus --oracle oracle.json
```

```console
policy 6ecdbc563f806f13, 66 messages graded by hand

kind            agrees   of      rate
deliberative        36   36   100.0%
mechanical          30   30   100.0%
overall             66   66   100.0%

every request went where the label says it should
```

A perfect score in this run. Jev is a live model, so your own grade may land a point or two lower; we've seen it miss two or three. The criteria were written specifically for this traffic, so we expected to get pretty good results.

Now let's add some traffic the criteria weren't written for. The repository carries twelve more families, every one of them touching money, and the team has a house rule about those:

```python
HOUSE_RULE = (
    "Anything touching money goes to the larger model, however mechanical it looks."
)
```

`policy.json` says nothing about money. Its criteria are about how much reasoning a request needs, not what a mistake would cost.

Let's ask Jev about that traffic plus sixteen ordinary requests from the corpus above, then grade everything against the house rule:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align oracle --corpus mixed --out mixed-oracle.json
```

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align grade --corpus mixed --oracle mixed-oracle.json
```

```console
policy 6ecdbc563f806f13, 40 messages graded by hand

kind                            agrees   of      rate
money, reads as deliberative        12   12   100.0%
money, reads as mechanical           1   12     8.3%
ordinary deliberative                8    8   100.0%
ordinary mechanical                  8    8   100.0%
overall                             29   40    72.5%

11 disagreements, the first 6:
  rename-charge-field  label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.99)
    Rename `chargeAmount` to `amount_cents` across billing/ and update the callers.
  rename-charge-field  label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.97)
    In billing/, `chargeAmount` should be `amount_cents` everywhere it appears.
  price-list-format    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.87)
    Convert this price list from JSON to YAML, keeping the key order.
  price-list-format    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.97)
    Turn the attached tariff JSON into equivalent YAML.
  refund-type-hints    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.78)
    Add type hints to every function in billing/refunds.py, including return types.
  refund-type-hints    label qwen-large  jev qwen-small (0.51)
    billing/refunds.py has no annotations. Add them.
```

Every ordinary request lands where its label says, and so do the finance-related tasks that obviously need thinking. Finance-related tasks that read as mechanical score one in twelve, and look at the confidence column: Jev is 0.99 sure that renaming a charge field is mechanical work.

Jev is reading the criteria correctly. The criteria just don't mention money, so the fix is to write the house rule into them.

You could do that by hand, and for one rule you probably should. [jev-align](https://github.com/sutro-sh/jev-align) does it from examples of your judgement instead: it shows you the requests Jev is least sure about, takes your label for each, and runs [GEPA](https://gepa-ai.github.io/gepa/) over your labels to propose new criteria.

> [!NOTE]
> If you want to see GEPA itself up close, the [GEPA lab](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=gepa-prompt-evolution&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme) walks through it. Our [Compiling prompts with DSPy](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=dspy-programs&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=jev-model-routing_readme) lab shows the other lever: keeping the wording and fitting the decision cut-offs from labelled examples instead.

jev-align asks you to label all forty requests, not just the twenty-four finance-related ones. The sixteen ordinary requests give the optimiser examples on both sides of the rule. If every example in the pool wanted `qwen-large`, it would learn to answer `qwen-large` every time.

Let's install jev-align, export the traffic, and generate the command that starts from the router's current policy:

```bash
uv tool install jev-align==0.1.4
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align export --corpus mixed --out pool.csv
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align seed --data pool.csv --batch-size 12
```

```console
wrote jeva-run.sh, which runs:

jeva optimize \
  pool.csv \
  --column message \
  --question 'Which model should answer `request.newest_message`? Judge only the newest message; `request.prior_turns` is context for what it refers to, never the thing being routed.' \
  --class 'qwen-small=The newest user message asks for a mechanical transformation that a competent engineer would finish without stopping to think: renaming or reformatting code, converting between two named formats, extracting values that are already written down in the message, translating prose, or answering a single factual question whose answer the message already contains. Length alone does not qualify a request for this option; a long but mechanical request still belongs here.' \
  --class 'qwen-large=The newest user message cannot be answered until something is worked out first: weighing a trade-off between two approaches, designing something that does not exist yet, diagnosing a fault from evidence that does not name the cause, reasoning about consequences the message does not state, or producing code whose correctness depends on a rule that has to be derived. Shortness does not disqualify a request from this option; a one-line question can still need deliberation.' \
  --jev-model 'jev-latest' \
  --batch-size 12 \
  --concurrency 6 \
  --max-metric-calls 120 \
  --reflection-model 'openrouter/anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5'

run it with `sh jeva-run.sh`; it asks you for every label.
```

The criteria in that command were read from `policy.json`, so the search starts from what the router is running today.

GEPA needs a model to write its proposals with. On a Zenable sandbox the generated command already names one. Anywhere else, put `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `GEMINI_API_KEY` in `~/.env` before running it, or pass `--reflection-model` naming any LiteLLM provider.

The script and `pool.csv` were written inside `router/`, so let's run it from there:

```bash
(cd router && sh jeva-run.sh)
```

`jeva` may first offer to upgrade itself; choose **Skip**, since the lab pins the version it was written against. Then it takes over the terminal. It shows one request at a time with how uncertain Jev is about it, you pick a label with the arrow keys, and it asks for a rationale you can skip. Twelve of those, then GEPA reads your labels and proposes new criteria.

Two models are at work here. Every score GEPA measures comes from Jev (`--jev-model jev-latest`) through the TypeSafe SDK, which reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` from your environment (`~/.env` on a sandbox). The new criteria are written by the `--reflection-model` in the generated command, which on a Zenable sandbox is the sandbox's hosted model (`anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5` above); GEPA calls it through LiteLLM, and the `openrouter/` prefix makes LiteLLM read `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and send those requests to openrouter.ai.

You accept or reject what it proposes. Read the proposal before accepting: a higher score on your own labels is expected, since those labels are what the score is measured against. A proposal identical to the criteria you started with means the search found nothing to change, which usually means you and the criteria already agree.

After you accept, `jeva` starts a second round of labels against the new criteria. You can stop there with Ctrl+C: it saves the run, and the criteria you accepted are already in it.

Once you've accepted one, let's install it into the router:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align adopt .jev-align/runs/<run-id>
```

<details>
<summary>Running without a Jev key?</summary>

Skip this if you adopted a run above. Without a key there's no run to adopt, so copy the criteria this loop produced when we ran it:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
cp router/jev_router/fixtures/policy-aligned.json router/jev_router/policy.json
```

Those shipped criteria came from this same search, with the labels written by a model applying the house rule rather than by a person. Yours will differ, and they should.

</details>

Either way, `policy.json` now holds different criteria, so its fingerprint has changed. Every cache entry and the oracle you built are filed under the old fingerprint, so the router asks Jev fresh rather than replaying stale answers. Let's grade again under the new criteria; the first line of the output shows the new fingerprint:

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align oracle --corpus mixed --out mixed-aligned.json
```

```bash
uv run --directory router python -m jev_router.align grade --corpus mixed --oracle mixed-aligned.json
```

```console
policy 0e5de277d72abdf3, 40 messages graded by hand

kind                            agrees   of      rate
money, reads as deliberative        12   12   100.0%
money, reads as mechanical          12   12   100.0%
ordinary deliberative                8    8   100.0%
ordinary mechanical                  7    8    87.5%
overall                             39   40    97.5%

1 disagreements, the first 1:
  add-type-hints       label qwen-small  jev qwen-large (0.99)
    Add type hints to every function in billing/refunds.py, including the return types, and use the buil
```

72.5% to 97.5%, and the row that moved is the one the rule was about: finance-related tasks that read as mechanical went from one in twelve to twelve out of twelve.

Now look at `ordinary mechanical`, which slipped from eight out of eight to seven. The request it lost was labelled `qwen-small` because adding type hints is mechanical, but it names `billing/refunds.py`. The criteria are applying the house rule correctly and the label is wrong: whoever labelled it looked at what the request does and missed which file it does it to. The fix is to the label, not the criteria, and a real traffic sample would surface a dozen of these on the first pass.

Question: the criteria now send finance-related tasks to the larger model, and ordinary requests still go where they went before. Which row of that table would show that the rewrite had gone too far?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`ordinary mechanical`. A rewrite that reached the money rule by widening what counts as serious work would drag renaming a variable and converting a JSON block along with it, and those are the requests the cheap model exists for.

`ordinary deliberative` can slip the other way, if the new criteria sort on money first and treat everything else as mechanical. That's why the pool has both ordinary halves in it: a pool of only finance-related requests would have scored "always use the larger model" at 100%.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Selecting a model for your task</summary>

Every grade in this section required that a human wrote a label ahead of time. A [NeurIPS 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15101) from Carnegie Mellon and Bilkent University proposes an approach, Cost-aware Majority Voting (CaMVo), that works without labelling beforehand.

Instead of sending each request to one model, it asks a few and takes a weighted vote. For each new request, it looks at similar requests it has already seen and how often each model's answer matched the final vote on them. Then it asks only the cheapest few models it expects, together, to get the answer right.

On the [MMLU benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300), CaMVo was more accurate than asking every model, at about 40% lower cost. On [IMDB movie reviews](https://huggingface.co/datasets/stanfordnlp/imdb), it halved the number of queries in exchange for a 0.17% accuracy loss, which may be a reasonable tradeoff between cost and quality.

</details>

## Route Claude Code through the gateway

_~10 min · Hands-on_

So far we've routed two local models behind an OpenAI-style endpoint. agentgateway also serves the Anthropic Messages API at `/v1/messages` on the same port, with the same ExtProc policy in front of it, so let's put Claude Code behind the router.

`03-claude-code.yaml` swaps the two Ollama entries for two hosted Claude models on OpenRouter and keeps the ExtProc block as it was:

```yaml
- name: sonnet
  provider: anthropic
  params:
    model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5
    baseUrl: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
    apiKey: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY
- name: opus
  provider: anthropic
  params:
    model: anthropic/claude-opus-5.5
    baseUrl: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
    apiKey: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY
```

The router needs criteria written for this pair of models, so it reads a second policy file. Same question, different options:

```json
{
  "question": "Which model should answer `request.newest_message`? Judge only the newest message; `request.prior_turns` is context for what it refers to, never the thing being routed.",
  "focus": "Decide on how much has to be worked out before the answer can start, not on the topic, the tone, or the length of `request.newest_message`. A request that names the exact change to make needs no deliberation even when the change is large. A request that states a goal and leaves the approach open needs deliberation even when it is one sentence.",
  "models": [
    {
      "name": "sonnet",
      "criterion": "The newest user message is well specified or straightforward: it names the files, the change, or the output it wants, and a competent engineer could carry it out without first choosing between approaches. Edits with a clear target, small features whose shape the message already gives, explanations of code that is in front of us, and questions with one checkable answer all belong here. Length alone does not disqualify a request from this option; a long but well-specified request still belongs here."
    },
    {
      "name": "opus",
      "criterion": "The newest user message leaves the approach open or needs something worked out before any change can start: designing a component or a migration, diagnosing a fault from symptoms that do not name the cause, weighing trade-offs between approaches, reviewing code for problems nobody has pointed at yet, or a change whose correct shape depends on parts of the codebase the message does not describe. Shortness does not disqualify a request from this option; a one-line goal can still need deliberation."
    }
  ]
}
```

`sonnet` is listed first, so it's also where a request goes when Jev runs out of time, the same way `qwen-small` was.

Now let's switch the router to the new policy and the gateway to the new config. The gateway reads the OpenRouter key from its environment at startup, so it gets recreated rather than restarted. It's also the first time the gateway calls out to the internet, and the sandbox only reaches it over IPv6, so we tell the gateway to look up IPv6 addresses only:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
sed -i '/JEV_FIXTURES/d' router.env
echo 'ROUTER_POLICY=policy-claude-code.json' >> router.env
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait jev-router
cp 03-claude-code.yaml config.yaml
export DNS_LOOKUP_FAMILY=V6Only
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait agentgateway
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'ext_proc listening' | tail -1
```

```console
11:00:14 INFO    jev_router.server ext_proc listening on 0.0.0.0:9090 | jev=jev-latest | deadline=1.5s | cache exact=True bucket=False ttl=900s | policy=23a97934d1f244ce
```

A different fingerprint, so nothing cached under the old criteria applies here.

Claude Code reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` for where to send requests, and `--model auto` goes into the request body as written; Claude Code warns that it doesn't know `auto`, then sends it anyway. `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` lowers the output cap it asks for, because Opus reserves credit against that cap before answering and the sandbox key's daily limit can't cover the default 32,000. Thinking counts against the same cap, so `--effort low` keeps it short enough to leave room for the answer.

Let's send one well-specified task and one open-ended one, both read-only:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=4096 ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000 claude -p --model auto --effort low "In router/jev_router/config.py, list every environment variable that RouterSettings.from_env reads, one per line, and nothing else."
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=4096 ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000 claude -p --model auto --effort low "The router in router/jev_router has no circuit breaker. How should we add one, and what would we measure before shipping it?"
```

```console
"auto" isn't described by this version's model catalog; update Claude Code, or map it with behavesAs on a modelPicker row …
[claude-code:unrecognized_model] {"model":"auto","query_source":"sdk"}
JEV_FIXTURES
JEV_BASE_URL
TYPESAFE_API_KEY
ROUTER_LISTEN
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL
JEV_MODEL
JEV_DEADLINE_SECONDS
ROUTER_STATE_MAX_CHARS
ROUTER_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS
ROUTER_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES
ROUTER_CACHE_EXACT
ROUTER_CACHE_BUCKET
ROUTER_CLAMP_UNKNOWN
ROUTER_ROUTED_MODEL
"auto" isn't described by this version's model catalog; …
[claude-code:unrecognized_model] {"model":"auto","query_source":"sdk"}
…
## Rollout

- Add `ROUTER_BREAKER_ENABLED` (default off), `ROUTER_BREAKER_THRESHOLD`, and `ROUTER_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_SECONDS` to `RouterSettings.from_env`, following the `_flag` pattern.
- Run it in shadow first: compute the breaker state and log "would have short-circuited", but still make the call. A week of that against real traffic gives you measurements 2 and 3 for free.
- Turn it on only if shadow mode shows trips lining up with real outages, not with isolated timeouts.
…
```

Let's check the routing logs and what the gateway sent on:

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
docker compose logs jev-router --no-log-prefix | grep 'src=jev' | tail -3
docker compose logs agentgateway --no-log-prefix | grep -o 'gen_ai.request.model=[^ ]*' | uniq -c
```

```console
11:08:32 INFO    jev_router.server route -> sonnet      src=jev      conf=1.00 {'sonnet': 1.0, 'opus': 0.0}
11:08:44 INFO    jev_router.server route -> opus        src=jev      conf=0.98 {'sonnet': 0.01, 'opus': 0.99}
11:11:34 INFO    jev_router.server route -> sonnet      src=jev      conf=0.10 {'sonnet': 0.55, 'opus': 0.45}
      3 gen_ai.request.model=anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5
      5 gen_ai.request.model=anthropic/claude-opus-5.5
      1 gen_ai.request.model=anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5
```

Jev asked once per prompt: the first went to Sonnet, the second to Opus. Every request after the first in a run carries tool results rather than new text, so the router keys those on the prompt that started the run, and the exact cache kept all five Opus requests on Opus. The last line is one more request Claude Code sent after the answer, with text of its own; Jev judged it separately and sent it to Sonnet, with little confidence either way.

> [!TIP]
> If Claude Code reports a `400` naming a field the gateway didn't forward, `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS=1` on the same command line removes the pre-release fields it sends to an Anthropic-format endpoint.

<details>
<summary>Doing the same without a gateway</summary>

The repository also carries `hack/auto-model`, a Claude Code plugin that asks once per session whether the task is Haiku, Sonnet or Opus grade and keeps every later request of that session on the answer. It's an alpha and no lab step uses it; `claude --plugin-dir ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing/hack/auto-model` tries it, and its README has the rest.

</details>

## Cleanup

_~2 min · Hands-on_

```bash
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/jev-model-routing
pkill -f jev_router.standin || true
docker compose down
rm -f router.env config.yaml mechanical.json deliberative.json standin.log
rm -f router/oracle.json router/mixed-oracle.json router/mixed-aligned.json router/pool.csv router/jeva-run.sh
rm -rf router/.jev-align
git checkout router/jev_router/policy.json
```

Then let's put Ollama back on loopback only:

```bash
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/listen.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart ollama
```

The two models stay on disk; `ollama rm qwen3:0.6b` and `ollama rm qwen3:1.7b` remove them if you want the space back. Thanks for building with us!
